cards.html: systemd can sandbox a service and cap its resources with a few lines in the unit, and no changes to the app. If the app is ever compromised, a hardened unit limits what the attacker can touch. If it leaks memory, a limit stops it from taking the whole server down with it.

systemd-analyze security scores every service from 0 (locked down) to 10 (fully exposed), and systemd-analyze security levelup lists each setting it checked. A fresh unit usually scores around 9 ("UNSAFE"). Adding the settings below typically brings a web app to about 2–4. Treat the score as a checklist, not a target: some settings break some apps.

• User= with a dedicated system user (chapter 4) is the baseline.
  • DynamicUser=yes goes further: systemd creates a throwaway user each time the service starts, and it switches on several protections automatically. Combine it with:
  • StateDirectory=levelup, which creates /var/lib/levelup owned by the service user, for data that must persist. Also CacheDirectory=, LogsDirectory= and RuntimeDirectory= (under /run, cleared on stop).

SettingWhat it doesBreaks
NoNewPrivileges=yesThe process and its children can never gain privileges (setuid binaries stop working)Apps that call sudo or setuid helpers
ProtectSystem=strictThe whole filesystem is read-only except /dev, /proc, /sysApps that write anywhere not listed below
ReadWritePaths=/opt/levelup/progressWritable exceptions to the above
ProtectHome=yes/home, /root and /run/user look emptyApps that read files in home directories
PrivateTmp=yesA private /tmp that other services can't seeSharing files through /tmp
PrivateDevices=yesNo access to physical devicesGPU or hardware access
ProtectKernelTunables=yes, ProtectKernelModules=yes, ProtectControlGroups=yesNo changes to kernel settings, modules or cgroupsAlmost nothing
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6Only normal network socketsApps using raw or netlink sockets

SettingWhat it doesBreaks
CapabilityBoundingSet= (empty)Drops all Linux capabilitiesApps that need, for example, port 80 as root
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICELets a non-root service bind ports below 1024
SystemCallFilter=@system-serviceAllows only system calls a normal service needsUnusual low-level software

cards.s: A hardened block for a Python web app
cards.html:
Add this to the [Service] section of the chapter 4 unit:

NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/opt/levelup/progress
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6
CapabilityBoundingSet=
SystemCallFilter=@system-service

Add settings a few at a time. After each step run daemon-reload and restart, exercise the app, and check journalctl -u levelup for "Permission denied" or "Read-only file system". Each error points at the setting to relax or the path to add to ReadWritePaths=.

These use the service's cgroup, so they cover every process the service starts:

SettingMeaning
MemoryHigh=400MSoft limit: above it, the kernel reclaims memory aggressively and slows the service down
MemoryMax=512MHard limit: above it, the kernel's out-of-memory killer kills a process in the service
CPUQuota=50%At most half of one CPU (200% = two CPUs)
CPUWeight= / IOWeight=A relative share when the machine is busy (default 100)
TasksMax=200At most 200 processes and threads: stops fork bombs and runaway threads
LimitNOFILE=65536Maximum open files and sockets per process; raise it for busy servers

When MemoryMax= is hit, the journal shows an out-of-memory kill, and with Restart=on-failure the service comes back. So a slow leak becomes a restart every few hours instead of a dead server. Fix the leak anyway.

Watch live use with systemd-cgtop, or for one service with systemctl status (the Memory, CPU and Tasks lines).

Services run in system.slice by default. You can create your own slice, for example apps.slice with MemoryMax=2G, and put several services in it with Slice=apps.slice. Together they can't use more than 2 GB, however the memory is split between them.

cards.s: Lab: harden the demo and hit a limit (VM, free)
cards.html:
1. systemd-analyze security demo and note the score.
  2. Add the hardened block above (with ReadWritePaths= set to a folder the demo writes to, or left out). Reload, restart and score it again.
  3. Add a /leak route to the demo that keeps appending 10 MB strings to a global list. Set MemoryMax=150M and Restart=on-failure.
  4. Call /leak in a loop, while true; do curl -s localhost:8000/leak; done, and watch journalctl -u demo -f. You will see the out-of-memory kill and the restart.
  5. Try ProtectHome=yes with an app that reads from /home/ubuntu to see what a permission error looks like in the journal.

1. What does systemd-analyze security measure?
  2. Your app fails with "Read-only file system" after you add ProtectSystem=strict. What is the fix?
  3. Which setting lets a non-root service listen on port 443?
  4. What is the difference between MemoryHigh= and MemoryMax=?
  5. Why add hardening settings a few at a time?
🔒 Answers: try the questions first, then tap to show

1: How exposed a service is, from 0 (locked down) to 10, based on its sandboxing settings. 2: Add the folder the app writes to with ReadWritePaths= (or use StateDirectory=). 3: AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE. 4: MemoryHigh slows the service by reclaiming memory; MemoryMax triggers the out-of-memory killer. 5: So when something breaks, you know which setting caused it.
